observation.visible_scene: A flat, snow-covered open field under overcast winter light, with sparse dark vegetation poking through the snow. A BBC logo sits in the top-left corner and a small numeral '6' in the top-right. The excerpt contains two shots separated by an editing cut: a dark gray wolf moving across the snow, then a bull elk with broad antlers facing the camera.
visible_changes: Frames 1-28: a single dark gray/black wolf, body oriented to the right, runs/trots across the snow with its legs cycling through a gait (alternating extended and gathered poses, tail streaming behind). The wolf stays roughly centered in frame while the blurred background vegetation shifts leftward across the frames, consistent with the camera panning to track the running animal.
The wolf's coat, build and right-facing orientation remain persistent throughout these frames; only its limb positions and slight body bob change.

At about t=2.24s (frame 29) there is a hard cut to a different subject: a large tan-bodied bull elk with a dark neck and wide branching antlers, standing/positioned facing the camera in the same snowy setting.

Frames 29-41: the elk remains the central subject, head held high, antlers spread; its legs shift slightly and its head/neck angle changes a little frame to frame, suggesting slow forward movement or an alert stance rather than a fast run. The background vegetation is mostly static relative to the elk, indicating little or no camera pan in this shot.
outside_clip_unknowns: Any causal or ecological relationship between the wolf and the elk (e.g., chase, hunt, or mere sequential footage) is not shown in this excerpt.
What the wolf was doing before t=0 and what happens after t=2.16s, and likewise the elk's actions before t=2.24s and after t=3.20s, are outside the cropped segment.
The reason for the cut between the two shots is not visible.
uncertain_details: Whether the wolf's apparent motion is its own running plus a camera pan, or primarily one of these, cannot be fully separated from the blurred background alone.
Whether the elk is walking toward the camera, standing still, or vocalizing (its mouth region is dark and ambiguous) is not certain from these frames.
The exact gait phase of the wolf and the precise stride of the elk vary frame to frame and are only partially resolved due to motion blur.

may already be underway in the first view and may continue beyond the last. The endpoints need
NOT match or connect as a loop. Do not judge different endpoints as a physical inconsistency,
and do not invent a trigger, contact, start, stop, landing, disappearance or completion to make
the excerpt form a complete story. Missing context outside this segment stays unknown.
If an editing cut is visible inside the segment, distinguish it from continuous physical motion;
do not invent a smooth transition or a causal mechanism to connect the two views.
Describe what is visible during the excerpt, the actual changes, and supported persistent
properties. Cover the main visible process, not just scenery. Distinguish object movement from
camera movement, reflection from separate objects, expansion from translation, deformation from
occlusion, and an already ongoing process from its onset. Only state what the clip supports;
do not invent causes, an earlier impact, an unseen operator, material identities or later outcomes.
Do not infer motion from one frame, a visible seam or a single pose. Static intervals are valid.
Do not supply named physics laws. Compare each important entity's first and last image positions
and their relative positions before describing motion. Treat camera motion as uncertain when the
background evidence is insufficient, and retain clear relative changes despite that uncertainty.
Return JSON {"visible_scene":"...", "visible_changes":["observation supported within the excerpt"],
